questions.prompt: Which particle has negative electric charge?
questions.explanation: Electrons are negative. Protons are positive and neutrons have no electric charge.

questions.prompt: Where are protons found in an atom?
options: Only in wires outside the atom.
In a separate cloud of negative electrons.
Only on the outside of a charged balloon.
questions.explanation: The nucleus is the central region containing protons and neutrons. Electrons occupy the surrounding region.

questions.prompt: What does electrically neutral mean?
options: There are no electrons or protons.
Positive and negative charges balance to give zero net charge.
questions.explanation: Neutral matter contains charged particles, but their charges cancel overall.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct unit symbol for electric charge?
questions.explanation: Charge is measured in coulombs, symbol C. A is ampere, V volt and Ω ohm.

questions.prompt: A selected patch has 8 protons and 9 electrons. What is its net charge?
questions.explanation: Eight positive and nine negative equal-sized elementary charges give 8 − 9 = −1.

questions.prompt: A selected patch has 8 protons and 6 electrons. What is its net charge?
questions.explanation: Its positive total exceeds its negative total by two elementary charges: 8 − 6 = +2.

questions.prompt: Which particle has no electric charge?
questions.explanation: A neutron is electrically neutral. An ion is an atom or group of atoms with net charge.

questions.prompt: How many coulombs is 1 μC?
questions.explanation: Micro means one millionth: 1 μC = 10⁻⁶ C. The prefix is different from milli, which is one thousandth.

questions.prompt: Approximately how many excess electrons give a charge of −1 C?
questions.explanation: The magnitude of one electron’s charge is about 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Divide 1 C by this magnitude to obtain about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons.

questions.prompt: Why can a neutral metal still conduct charge?
options: Neutral means it has no particles.
It has mobile electrons, despite having zero net charge overall.
All its protons move freely between atoms.
questions.explanation: Conductivity depends on mobile carriers, not a pre-existing net charge. The positive ion cores and electrons can balance while some electrons remain mobile.

questions.prompt: In the chosen balloon–cloth model, which particles transfer to the balloon?
questions.explanation: The model transfers electrons from cloth to balloon; the positive nuclei stay in their materials.

questions.prompt: What happens to a neutral balloon when it gains electrons?
options: Its net charge must stay zero.
questions.explanation: Adding negative charge produces a negative imbalance if the positive total stays unchanged.

questions.prompt: What happens to the cloth when it loses electrons to the balloon?
options: It becomes a pure electron gas.
questions.explanation: Losing negative electrons leaves a positive excess. Positive charge does not require protons to move into the cloth.

questions.prompt: What does conservation of charge mean for an isolated pair?
options: Neither object can ever change charge.
Its total charge stays the same.
Rubbing creates equal amounts of new matter.
Only the negative total is conserved.
questions.explanation: Charge can transfer between the objects while the total of the isolated system stays unchanged.

questions.prompt: Two initially neutral patches exchange three electrons from cloth to balloon. What are their net charges?
questions.explanation: Three negative elementary charges leave one patch and enter the other. The total is still zero.

questions.prompt: Which statement about rubbing is correct?
options: Friction manufactures new electrons from energy in every case.
Protons always move from cloth into plastic.
Every rubbed material must become negative.
Contact and separation can transfer existing electrons.
questions.explanation: The transferred electrons already exist. The direction depends on the material pair and surface conditions.

questions.prompt: What does static mean in static electricity?
options: A charge imbalance persists without a continuous circuit current.
Electrons can never move at any stage.
Only positively charged matter is present.
questions.explanation: Static charge can move while an object is charging, redistributing charge or discharging. Static does not mean charge is permanently immobile.

questions.prompt: An isolated pair starts with total charge zero. One object finishes at +2 μC. What is the other object’s charge?
questions.explanation: Conservation requires the two final charges to add to the initial zero total.

questions.prompt: Why is an object positive after electron loss, even though no proton entered?
options: Losing matter always produces positive charge.
Its unchanged positive charge now exceeds its negative charge.
Positive charge is made by rubbing air.
questions.explanation: Net charge is the signed sum. Removing negative charge leaves an imbalance in favour of the positive total already present.

questions.prompt: An isolated pair initially totals +1 μC. After contact, one object is −2 μC. What is the other?
questions.explanation: The total remains +1 μC. The other charge must satisfy −2 + Q = +1, so Q = +3 μC.

questions.prompt: How do two negative net charges interact?
options: They exert no force because both are negative.
questions.explanation: Like net charges repel: negative–negative and positive–positive.

questions.prompt: How do opposite net charges interact?
options: They always become neutral without transfer.
They cannot interact across a gap.
questions.explanation: Opposite charge signs attract. A force can act without direct contact.

questions.prompt: What is an electrical force?
options: A quantity measured only in coulombs per second.
A push or pull associated with charge.
The number of neutrons in an atom.
questions.explanation: Force is a push or pull. Electrical forces are associated with charge and can act across a space.

questions.prompt: What does polarisation mean here?
options: Turning every neutron into an electron.
Requiring the object to acquire a non-zero net charge.
A small redistribution of charge within an object.
questions.explanation: Charges shift slightly so opposite charge can be nearer an external charged object; the polarised object can remain neutral overall.

questions.prompt: Why can a negative balloon attract a neutral wall?
options: The wall’s charge distribution shifts, with positive charge effectively nearer.
The wall must always have a negative net charge.
The balloon sends new protons through the wall.
questions.explanation: Polarisation puts opposite charge closer. That attraction can outweigh the more distant like-charge repulsion.

questions.prompt: Does attraction prove that a nearby object has the opposite net charge?
options: No; a neutral object can be polarised and attracted.
Yes, because neutral objects have no charges inside.
questions.explanation: Both an oppositely charged object and a neutral polarised object can be attracted.

questions.prompt: Which observation best supports a like net charge in this introductory rod test?
options: Attraction to a known charged rod alone.
The rod being the same colour.
Repulsion from a rod with known charge.
questions.explanation: Repulsion provides stronger evidence of like charge. Attraction alone can also occur through polarisation of neutral matter.

questions.prompt: For unchanged point charges in air, what generally happens as separation increases?
options: The magnitude of electric force decreases.
questions.explanation: For the point-charge idealisation, force magnitude is proportional to 1/r². The force arrows in our introductory lab are qualitative.

questions.prompt: A neutral object is polarised beside a charged one, with no charge transferred. What is its total charge?
options: Equal to the charged object’s charge.
questions.explanation: Redistribution changes position, not the signed total, when no charge enters or leaves.

questions.prompt: Two like charged rods are moved further apart. Which statement is consistent?
options: They must begin attracting at any larger distance.
They still repel, usually with a weaker force.
Their protons leave through the air.
questions.explanation: Changing distance changes force magnitude without necessarily changing net charge or whether the interaction attracts or repels.

questions.prompt: What makes a metal a good conductor?
options: Its protons travel around a circuit freely.
It contains no charges at all.
It has mobile charge carriers, including electrons.
questions.explanation: Some electrons in a metal can move through it; the positive ion cores remain part of the lattice.

questions.prompt: Why can charge persist on a dry plastic comb?
options: Its protons are moving faster than light.
Plastic does not let charge move through it easily.
questions.explanation: An insulator does not readily conduct charge through its bulk, so a surface imbalance can persist.

questions.prompt: Which is normally a good electrical conductor?
questions.explanation: Copper has mobile electrons. These dry insulating materials do not conduct nearly as readily under ordinary conditions.

questions.prompt: What is a lattice in this lesson?
options: An organised arrangement of particles in a solid.
A single electron in empty space.
questions.explanation: Metal ion cores occupy positions in a solid lattice and vibrate around those positions.

questions.prompt: What usually moves through a metal earth wire?
options: Protons migrating from nucleus to nucleus.
questions.explanation: Electronic conduction in metal involves mobile electrons; positive ion cores do not travel along the wire.

questions.prompt: Can a neutral copper wire carry current?
options: No, it must first lose all electrons.
Yes, because its protons flow through the circuit.
Yes, its mobile electrons can drift while it stays nearly neutral overall.
questions.explanation: A wire can have balanced overall charge and still support a directed flow of mobile electrons.

questions.prompt: Why might humid conditions reduce some static effects?
options: Moisture can provide paths for charge to leak away.
Humidity turns all matter into a perfect conductor.
Protons stop having charge in damp air.
questions.explanation: The leakage depends on surface and environmental conditions. The point is a possible discharge path, not disappearance of charge.

questions.prompt: Why does touching one patch of a charged insulator with an earth lead not guarantee complete discharge?
options: The Earth cannot ever accept electrons.
Charge cannot readily move from all other patches to that contact.
The wire’s protons must first become electrons.
questions.explanation: Local contact may discharge a patch, but poor bulk and surface conduction can keep remote charge in place.

questions.prompt: Which comparison separates conductivity from net charge?
options: Every charged object is automatically a good conductor.
A neutral metal can conduct while a charged plastic surface can retain local charge.
An insulator must be neutral at all times.
questions.explanation: Net charge is an imbalance; conductivity describes mobility. They are different properties.

questions.prompt: Why are the positive ion cores not shown circulating with electrons in a metal?
options: Their positive charge has no force.
They disappear as soon as current starts.
Every metal nucleus is actually neutral.
They remain bound in the lattice, although they vibrate.
questions.explanation: The metal’s structure holds the ion cores in the solid. Mobile electrons carry the net drift current.

questions.prompt: What is earthing a metal object?
options: Connecting it to Earth by a conducting path.
questions.explanation: An earth connection allows charge transfer between the conducting object and the large charge reservoir of Earth.

questions.prompt: A negative metal sphere is earthed with no nearby charging object. Which way do excess electrons move?
options: From the sphere’s nuclei into new protons.
questions.explanation: The sphere’s excess electrons can flow through the conducting lead into Earth until the isolated imbalance is removed.

questions.prompt: A positive metal sphere is earthed with no nearby charging object. Which way can electrons move?
options: Only from the insulating stand to the air.
Electrons cannot respond to a positive object.
questions.explanation: The electron deficit can be filled from Earth through the conducting connection.

questions.prompt: What is an electrical discharge?
options: A continuous current in every object forever.
Transfer of charge that reduces or redistributes an imbalance.
questions.explanation: A discharge transfers existing charge. A spark is one visible form of discharge through air.

questions.prompt: Why is the metal sphere mounted on an insulating stand in the model?
options: To stop an unintended conducting path to the surroundings.
To provide a second metal wire to Earth.
To make the sphere have no atoms.
To increase the number of protons by rubbing.
questions.explanation: The stand helps the isolated sphere retain charge until the intended lead is attached.

questions.prompt: A sufficiently strong electric field can make air do what?
options: Turn every electron into light with no charge left.
questions.explanation: Electrical breakdown can make air conduct. Charge transfer through the conducting region can produce light, sound and heating.

questions.prompt: What does bonding conducting fuel-handling parts aim to reduce?
options: The number of nuclei in the fuel.
Potential differences and the risk of a spark between them.
All chemical energy in the fuel.
questions.explanation: Bonding provides an electrical link between conducting parts; engineered procedures reduce spark risk. This is not a fuel-handling activity for students.

questions.prompt: How does bonding differ from earthing?
options: Bonding creates electrons; earthing creates protons.
They are names for opposite charge signs.
Bonding joins conducting objects; earthing connects to Earth.
questions.explanation: The purposes can overlap in systems, but an inter-object connection and a connection to Earth are distinct ideas.

questions.prompt: A selected sphere has 8 positive cores and 11 electrons. After ideal earthing without external influences, how many selected electrons balance those cores?
questions.explanation: Three excess electrons leave in the simplified selected-patch model, leaving 8 positives and 8 negatives.

questions.prompt: Why is a shortest-path-only rule insufficient to predict lightning?
options: Lightning can flow only through plastic.
Air breakdown and electric-field conditions determine a complex route.
Charge cannot move through ionised air.
questions.explanation: Lightning paths are more complex than a geometric shortest line; it may occur within clouds as well as to ground.

questions.prompt: What helps a photocopier place toner on selected regions?
options: Making the entire page a magnet only.
questions.explanation: Toner particles respond to controlled charge patterns, then the image is transferred and fixed.

questions.prompt: What can electrostatic spray painting use?
options: A continuous supply of new charge created from nothing.
Attraction of charged droplets to a suitably connected workpiece.
questions.explanation: Electrostatic forces can assist deposition, while repulsion between similarly charged droplets can help spread a spray.

questions.prompt: What is the main target of an electrostatic precipitator?
options: Suspended particles in a gas stream.
questions.explanation: Charged particles are attracted towards collecting surfaces. This does not guarantee removal of gaseous pollutants.

questions.prompt: Which is an everyday example of electrostatic discharge?
options: A book simply resting on a table.
A brief spark after walking on carpet and touching metal.
A wooden ruler measuring a length.
questions.explanation: Contact and separation can charge a person; touching a conductor can allow a brief discharge.

questions.prompt: What makes a charged dust collector useful?
options: Electrical forces can direct charged particles towards a collection surface.
It blocks all gases by turning them into protons.
questions.explanation: The charge helps separate suspended material from flowing gas, but collection and later removal are still needed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a defibrillator is most accurate?
options: It is simply a charged comb attracting the heart.
It restarts every heart regardless of rhythm.
It removes all electrons from a patient.
It delivers a controlled electrical pulse for certain abnormal heart rhythms.
questions.explanation: A defibrillator concerns stored electrical energy and a controlled current pulse; it is not merely electrostatic attraction or a universal restart device.

questions.prompt: Why can clothing cling after drying?
options: Contact and separation can produce charge imbalances and attraction.
Fabric atoms have lost all nuclei.
Every item has exactly the same net charge and must attract.
Only gravity can act between fabrics.
questions.explanation: Dry insulating materials can retain charge. Attraction may involve opposite charges or polarisation.

questions.prompt: What keeps the pizza analogy distinct from static attraction?
options: Static attraction requires a steady closed metal loop.
The circuit model represents a continuing current in a closed loop.
The pizza model has no energy transfer.
Static charge has no electric forces.
questions.explanation: Static examples concern a persisting imbalance; a driven circuit can sustain current and energy transfer.

questions.prompt: Why should an industrial particle filter not be described as removing all pollution?
options: It cannot attract any charged matter.
It targets particles and does not necessarily capture gaseous pollutants.
questions.explanation: Particles and gaseous pollutants are different. A particular separation method addresses specific materials.

questions.prompt: Which statement connects static and circuit electricity correctly?
options: Static electricity contains only protons; circuits only neutrons.
Charge exists only when a switch is closed.
Circuit charge is always created by the battery.
Both involve charge, but their arrangements and patterns of movement differ.
questions.explanation: The same charge concepts underlie both. A battery supplies energy and maintains conditions for flow; rubbing can redistribute existing charge.
